Making an excellent design system legible

A self-initiated study of Stripe's checkout theming. The components held under every stress I could build. What didn't hold was the merchant's view of them: the system edits their brand, enforces limits, and picks languages on their behalf, and tells them none of it.

Overview

Most design system case studies are written from inside a team that shares a Figma library and a Slack channel. Stripe's checkout has a harder job. It ships to thousands of businesses who share none of that context. They recolour it, restyle it, and drop it into their own page and their own market, and they cannot see inside it. So the question isn't whether the components are well built. It is where Stripe's system stops, where the merchant's begins, and what a merchant knows about what they just shipped.

At a glance
  • Role: Research, synthesis, interaction design, prototyping
  • Type: Self-initiated, no affiliation with Stripe
  • Duration: One week
  • Method: A sandbox built against Stripe's test mode, measured in Brave
  • Outcome: Four findings backed by measurement, and three concept screens answering them
The problem

Stripe's checkout is the most interesting design system problem I know of. The merchant's designer owns the brand, has a colour and a typeface and a set of rules, and wants the payment step to feel like the rest of the experience. They will never see Stripe's source, and they mostly won't test the checkout in another language. The merchant's developer implements the theme inside a setup where brand values live in one place and everything points at them, ships, and moves on.

The shopper notices none of this, unless something looks wrong, in which case they notice it as doubt, at the exact moment they are being asked for a card number. The design question sits between the first two: what does a merchant know about what they just shipped?

How I tested it

I gave myself one merchant's brand and tried to break it. The sandbox renders Stripe's real payment form live and launches Stripe's hosted page with matching settings, so the two surfaces can be compared side by side. Where I could, I stopped judging by eye and measured what rendered: padding values, computed contrast, which typeface each script resolved to.

The sandbox is not a Stripe product but it uses Stripe's test keys to load Stripe's real payment form, so every finding is about Stripe's actual component. It exists because Stripe offers nothing like it: its Branding page previews one condition, and merchants who theme the embedded form in code get no preview at all.

The matrix I pushed it through

  • Theme: Hot pink, hard shadows, pill shapes, and a left padding rule written the way an English-speaking office writes one.
  • Typeface: Playfair Display, which has no Arabic letters, against Noto Kufi Arabic and the system font.
  • Language: English, German, Japanese, and Arabic, which reads right to left and mirrors the whole form.
  • Currency: Five, including yen, which has no decimal places, and dinar, which has three.

The biggest gap in this study is that there are no merchant interviews yet. Every claim comes from Stripe's public documentation or a measurement in the sandbox. Anything I could not verify was left out.

Components

The components are excellent. I could not break them. Arabic and right-to-left, multiple currencies, no-decimal currencies, crowded payment lists in two layouts, phone width, all held up. The problems are not in the components. They are in what a merchant can see, control, and connect to.

A loud theme, hot pink, hard shadows, pill shapes, still coherent.

The same theme in Arabic. Labels, inputs, tabs, and icons all mirror.

The one exception: a Latin-only font in Arabic. Two typefaces, neither chosen.

Findings

Stripe's system constantly makes decisions on the merchant's behalf: ignoring a value it cannot read, enforcing a limit, picking a language. The system is less controllable than merchants assume, and it says almost none of it out loud.

That reframed the project. I started this project expecting to redesign components. The actual opportunity arose where a specific theme gets chosen. For hosted Checkout, it previews a single condition. For the embedded form, where most of these findings are, there is no editor at all. The merchant's developer themes it in code and learns about the failures in a console.

1. A company keeps its brand colour in one place, and every button on every page points at it. Change it once, and the whole site follows. I tried to point Stripe's checkout at that same source, the way a developer points everything else, and Stripe refused:

The colour has to be typed in manually, as #FF3D7F. So it now lives in two places, and when the brand changes, one of them gets forgotten. Translucent colours are refused outright: rgb() is accepted, rgba() is not, so a brand built on soft overlays has to drop them at the payment step.

What happens next is the checkout still loads, in Stripe's own brand color rather than the merchant's pink, and the only error is a line in the console. A store can run for months with a payment page that carries none of its brand, and the merchant is never notified.

2. Stripe lets a merchant restyle the checkout by naming its pieces: the input boxes, the labels above them, the payment method tabs. Each piece accepts a fixed set of changes, mostly colour, spacing, borders and corner rounding. Ask for anything outside that set and it is dropped. No error, no warning. The form renders as if the instruction was never written.

The limit itself is right. A payment form that a merchant can reshape freely can break easily.

The problem is that merchants are told they can theme their checkout. They are never shown where theming stops, so a designer hands over a spec, a developer writes it, and both assume it shipped but only half of it does.

3. A checkout is not only the merchant's brand. Apple Pay is black, Link is green, Klarna is pink, Amazon is yellow, and Visa, Mastercard and Amex each bring their own mark. None of them can be recoloured, and they should not be: a shopper needs to recognise the button that holds their card. Stripe also adds its own elements, like a green cashback badge on the bank option, which the merchant never asked for and cannot remove.

With card payments only, the checkout looks like the merchant. If a merchant turns on nine payment methods, which any shop selling across Europe does, the page becomes a wall of other companies' logos with the merchant's pink button at the bottom. Nothing changes this and the merchant is given no warning about it.

4. A shopper in Dubai with an English phone taps Arabic on a merchant's site. Everything turns Arabic until the payment step, which stays English. Not because Arabic is unsupported, with the browser set to Arabic the hosted page rendered beautifully. The merchant simply cannot ask for it.

The hosted page accepts forty locales, none of them right to left. Stripe's embedded form accepts Arabic directly.

The design

Stress preview in the Branding page

Today, Stripe's Branding page shows the merchant's theme in exactly one condition: English, US dollars, card only, desktop. That is the condition least likely to break.

Today. Stripe's Branding page: two colour pickers, one preview, no contrast warning.

The proposal: the same page, with the merchant's theme rendered live in the four conditions nobody tests before launch, right to left, a no-decimal currency, a crowded payment list, phone width. It is buildable with what Stripe already has: the same payment form, rendered four times with different settings.

Checks at the point of choosing

A font picker that knows which languages a merchant serves, and says when a face has no letters for one of them.

The same pattern applies to colour. My own test theme's pink button puts white text at roughly 3.4:1 contrast, under the accessibility standard for body text. The system can already compute this and I got no warning while I was picking it.

Make the language gap legible

If the hosted page cannot offer Arabic, the system should say so where a merchant would look, next to what their shopper will actually get, with the alternative.

Stripe should support the four right-to-left languages on both surfaces. This screen is what I would design for the interim.
